items.title: Rigid Shell
items.question: What is the outer, rigid layer of the Earth that is broken into moving plates called?
items.correctExplanation: Right. This cool, brittle shell rides on a hotter, slowly deforming layer beneath it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the lithosphere. It includes the crust and the uppermost rigid mantle, unlike the softer layer below.
items.lessonContent:
Layers can be defined by rigidity, not just depth.
Brittle shells can fracture and move.
Identify the layer by behaviour.
Distinguish similar-sounding geospheres.
Share this: name one material whose behaviour depends on temperature.

items.title: Soft Layer Below
items.question: On what layer do tectonic plates effectively glide?
items.correctExplanation: Right. This hotter, weaker layer deforms slowly and allows the rigid plates above to move.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the asthenosphere. Its ductile behaviour provides the lubrication plates need to shift.
items.lessonContent:
Movement needs a deforming substrate.
Softer layers enable rigid slabs to slide.
Temperature controls mechanical behaviour.
Match a motion to its mechanism.
Share this: find one system that moves because something beneath it yields.

items.title: Pulling Apart
items.question: What kind of boundary forms where two plates move away from each other?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Spreading plates create new crust along ridges as material rises to fill the gap.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a divergent boundary. Moving apart allows magma to rise and solidify into fresh crust.
items.lessonContent:
Boundary types follow plate motion.
Moving apart creates new material.
Rising material fills the opening.
Classify by relative movement.
Share this: name one process where separation creates something new.

items.title: Pushing Together
items.question: What is created where an ocean plate meets a continental plate and sinks beneath it?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The denser ocean plate descends, producing deep trenches and chains of volcanoes.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a subduction zone. Sinking crust melts at depth and fuels the volcanism above it.
items.lessonContent:
Density decides which plate sinks.
Sinking crust drives melting and volcanism.
Trenches mark the descent.
Connect motion to surface features.
Share this: name one place where something denser sinks beneath something lighter.

items.title: Side by Side
items.question: What is a boundary where two plates slide past each other horizontally called?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Here crust is neither created nor destroyed; the plates simply grind past one another.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a transform boundary. Sliding motion builds stress that releases as earthquakes rather than as new crust or volcanoes.
items.lessonContent:
Some boundaries neither build nor destroy.
Horizontal motion stores stress.
Stress release appears as shaking.
Classify by the kind of motion.
Share this: name one system that stores energy by sliding rather than colliding.

items.title: New Sea Floor
items.question: What process creates new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Magma rises at the ridge, solidifies, and pushes older crust outward on both sides.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is seafloor spreading. The pattern of magnetic stripes records this steady outward growth.
items.lessonContent:
New material forms where plates separate.
Outward growth pushes older parts away.
Symmetry around a ridge reveals the process.
Use patterns as evidence of motion.
Share this: notice one record that preserves a repeated process.

items.title: Single Landmass
items.question: What is the name of the ancient supercontinent that later broke apart?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Matching coastlines, fossils, and rocks across oceans record its break-up.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Pangaea. The matching evidence on separate continents is what first suggested the land had once been joined.
items.lessonContent:
Present features can preserve past connections.
Matching evidence across gaps signals former unity.
Reconstruct history from scattered clues.
Weigh multiple lines of evidence.
Share this: find one sign that two separate things were once joined.

items.title: Fossil Match
items.question: Why do identical fossils appear on continents now separated by an ocean?
choices: The ocean was once dry land
items.correctExplanation: Right. Distributed species could not cross wide oceans, so the land must have been connected when they lived.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the continents were once joined. Matching fossils across wide water is strong evidence of former proximity.
items.lessonContent:
Distribution puzzles imply past connections.
Organisms that cannot cross water suggest a land bridge.
Combine geology with biology.
Use inexplicable facts as clues.
Share this: find one fact best explained by a past connection.

items.title: Driving Motion
items.question: What mainly drives the movement of tectonic plates?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Heat from the interior sets up slow circulation that carries plates along with it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is convection in the mantle. Rising hot rock and sinking cool rock transfer heat and momentum to the plates above.
items.lessonContent:
Heat differences drive circulation.
Moving fluids can carry solid cargo.
Slow motions can still be powerful.
Connect a driver to the motion it causes.
Share this: name one system powered by a temperature difference.

items.title: Rocks Break
items.question: What causes most earthquakes at plate boundaries?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Stress builds where rock is stuck, then releases suddenly when it breaks and slides.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is sudden slip along a fault. The stored elastic energy radiates as seismic waves when the rock finally moves.
items.lessonContent:
Stress accumulates at locked boundaries.
Sudden release radiates energy.
Stored strain explains sudden events.
Link a slow build-up to a fast release.
Share this: name one event caused by stored pressure releasing.

items.title: Underground Origin
items.question: What is the point inside the Earth where an earthquake begins called?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The focus lies at depth, while the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the focus. Confusing it with the surface point reverses the relationship between depth and the map location.
items.lessonContent:
Interior origins project to surface points.
Distinguish depth from map location.
Define terms precisely.
Relate an object to its projection.
Share this: distinguish the source of an event from where it is felt.

items.title: Surface Point
items.question: What is the point on the surface directly above an earthquake's origin called?
items.correctExplanation: Right. It marks where the released energy is usually felt most strongly.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the epicentre. It sits on the surface, directly above the deeper point where the rupture occurred.
items.lessonContent:
Surface projections name a separate point.
Locate both origin and projection.
Map coordinates need a reference.
Relate depth to surface location.
Share this: mark where one deep event would be felt at the surface.

items.title: Two Wave Types
items.question: Which seismic waves arrive first at a distant station?
items.correctExplanation: Right. These compressional waves travel fastest, so they are recorded before the others.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is primary waves. Their speed advantage is why the arrival order of wave types reveals distance to the origin.
items.lessonContent:
Speed differences create arrival order.
Timing reveals distance.
Use sequence as a measuring tool.
Fast signals arrive before slow ones.
Share this: use an arrival delay to estimate one distance.

items.title: Seismic Strength
items.question: What does earthquake magnitude measure?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Magnitude is a single figure for the source, while damage varies with distance and local conditions.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is energy released at the source. Confusing it with local damage mixes a source property with a site effect.
items.lessonContent:
Source and site effects differ.
One number may describe the origin only.
Damage depends on more than strength.
Separate cause from local impact.
Share this: distinguish the strength of an event from its local effects.

items.title: Tidal Wave
items.question: What usually generates a tsunami?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Sudden vertical movement of the seabed pushes the whole water column, sending long waves across the ocean.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is displacement of the seafloor. The wave travels through the full depth of water, which is why it crosses oceans with little loss.
items.lessonContent:
Large water waves need a large sudden push.
Deep disturbance carries energy far.
Distinguish wind waves from displaced-water waves.
Connect cause to scale.
Share this: name one hazard caused by a sudden vertical shift.

items.title: Where Plates Sink
items.question: What deep feature typically marks a subduction zone?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The descending plate bends the seafloor down, producing the deepest parts of the oceans.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an ocean trench. The bend at the point of descent creates a long, narrow depression.
items.lessonContent:
Sinking creates a deep low.
Map features reveal underlying motion.
Connect a landform to a process.
Read topography as evidence.
Share this: link one deep feature to the process that shaped it.

items.title: Underwater Chain
items.question: What long feature forms where plates pull apart on the ocean floor?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Rising magma builds a long elevated chain along the spreading boundary.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a mid-ocean ridge. New crust added at the boundary creates a raised ridge that runs for thousands of kilometres.
items.lessonContent:
Spreading raises new terrain.
Growth leaves a raised seam.
Long features follow long boundaries.
Connect creation to topography.
Share this: find one feature created by material being added.

items.title: Magnetic Record
items.question: What do the alternating magnetic stripes on the seafloor record?
items.correctExplanation: Right. New crust locks in the field direction at the time it forms, creating a striped record as the field flips.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is reversals of Earth's magnetic field. The symmetrical pattern on both sides of a ridge also confirms spreading.
items.lessonContent:
Some materials record conditions when they form.
Symmetry reveals a shared origin.
Natural archives preserve history.
Read patterns as timelines.
Share this: name one natural record that stores past conditions.

items.title: Hawaii Chain
items.question: A chain of volcanoes forms over a stationary deep source as a plate moves. What is that source called?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The plate drifts over a fixed plume, leaving a line of progressively older volcanoes.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a hot spot. The age progression along the chain shows the plate moving over a stationary source.
items.lessonContent:
Fixed sources leave trails.
Age order along a chain reveals motion.
Relative motion explains patterns.
Use progressions as evidence.
Share this: find one trail that records something moving over time.

items.title: Building Mountains
items.question: What process raises large mountain ranges such as the Himalayas?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Where two continental plates meet, the crust crumples and thickens into high ranges.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is collision of continental plates. Neither plate sinks easily, so the crust piles up instead.
items.lessonContent:
Collisions can lift terrain.
When neither side sinks, material piles up.
Connect compression to elevation.
Read ranges as evidence of collision.
Share this: name one feature formed by two things pressing together.

items.title: Splitting a Continent
items.question: What feature forms where a continent is being pulled apart?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Stretching thins the crust and drops a long block down between faults.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a rift valley. Tension pulls the crust apart, and the sunken block becomes a long depression.
items.lessonContent:
Tension thins and drops crust.
Stretching creates lows, not highs.
Match a landform to its stress.
Contrast compression and tension.
Share this: contrast one feature made by pulling with one made by pushing.

items.title: Ring of Fire
items.question: Why are so many volcanoes and earthquakes concentrated around the Pacific Rim?
choices: It is closest to the equator
The core is nearer the surface
items.correctExplanation: Right. Several plates converge along the rim, producing frequent subduction, volcanism, and quakes.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is many plate boundaries meet there. Concentration of hazards follows concentration of plate interaction.
items.lessonContent:
Hazards cluster where boundaries cluster.
Geography follows underlying structure.
Look for a common cause behind a pattern.
Map activity to detect structure.
Share this: find one pattern explained by a shared underlying cause.

items.title: Slow Drift
items.question: How fast do tectonic plates typically move each year?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The pace matches the growth of a fingernail, yet over millions of years it reshapes the planet.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a few centimetres. Imperceptibly slow motion accumulates into enormous change across geological time.
items.lessonContent:
Slow rates can produce large results.
Time multiplies small movements.
Do not equate slow with insignificant.
Estimate cumulative effects.
Share this: compute one huge result from a tiny annual change.

items.title: Inner Heat
items.question: Where does most of the Earth's internal heat come from today?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The decay of long-lived isotopes, plus leftover primordial heat, keeps the interior hot.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is radioactive decay in the interior. This steady source drives the convection that moves plates.
items.lessonContent:
Internal heat needs an internal source.
Decay supplies energy over long timescales.
Trace a driver to its origin.
Distinguish surface from interior energy.
Share this: identify the source behind one long-lived process.

items.title: Ocean Age
items.question: Why is oceanic crust generally much younger than continental crust?
choices: It is continually recycled by subduction
It was formed more recently by humans
It is made of younger minerals only
items.correctAnswer: It is continually recycled by subduction
items.correctExplanation: Right. Dense ocean plates sink back into the mantle, so little ancient seafloor survives.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it is continually recycled by subduction. Continental crust is buoyant enough to avoid the same fate.
items.lessonContent:
Recycling resets ages.
What can be destroyed does not accumulate.
Buoyancy decides what survives.
Explain age distributions by process.
Share this: name one material whose age reflects constant renewal.
